chapter_theme: Songs at Thiruparankundram (திருப்பரங்குன்றம்): the poet confesses his bondage to women, courtesans who take a man's wealth with false hearts, his neglect of worship, his life from the womb to disease, and his begging from patrons, and asks for Murugan's feet, while the praise turns on the hunter girl, the vel against Sura, Vishnu as uncle and Murugan as teacher of Siva.
structure_note: All but 11 and 13 follow the two halves: confession and plea, then praise ending at the shrine. The confessions are mostly of women (7, 10, 12, 14, 16 to 20); 8 confesses neglected worship and asks for help at death, 9 runs through a life from conception, 15 confesses begging.

7.reading: The poet describes, frankly and at length, lovemaking with proud women, from stroking their feet and loosening their clothes to biting, nail marks and the cries of birds, and asks whether he will ever give up delighting in it. He praises Murugan as Saravanabhava who told the Rig mantra to the seven sages, who wears on his shoulders Tamil poems that spread grammar and music, and as the holy child of the guru who gave grace under the kuruntham tree to the devotees of Sankara who danced in the hall.
7.nuance: தவிர்வேனோ, 'will I give it up?', is the whole plea: the confession is the bulk of the song. திருக்குருந்தடி அருள்பெற அருளிய குருநாதர் recalls Siva as the guru under the kuruntham tree, a story told of Manikkavasagar; the following lines (குருக்களின் திறம்) make Murugan the guru of gurus, and their syntax is not certain.

8.reading: The poet confesses that he has not worshipped Murugan daily, told his nature, bowed at his feet with flowers, done any austerity, sought out his devotees, gone round his hill or praised him with joy; and asks that when Death's men come on the bellowing buffalo with noose and club and his mind fails, Murugan come at that moment on the peacock and end his fear. The praise names the vel that slew the demons while ghouls leapt and vultures fed, the hunter girl's kumkum on his shoulders, and the sages of the four Vedas who worship him daily at Parangiri.
8.nuance: The confession is a list of omitted worship (தொழுதிலன், பணிந்திலன், வருகிலன்), and the plea is for one moment only, the hour of death. மறலிதன் உழையினர் are Death's servants, with the noose (கயிறு) and club (கதை) and Yama's buffalo (பகடு). This hour-of-death plea recurs through the book.

9.reading: The poet traces his life from the embryo ten months in the womb, through birth, washing, nursing, crawling and the child's ornaments, to youth, friendship with women and wandering in disease, and asks when he will gain the mind of Murugan's grace. The praise tells how the gods came to earth as Rama's monkey and bear army, the sun and Indra as monkey kings, Brahma as lord of the bears, Agni as Nila and Rudra as Hanuman, and names Murugan as nephew of Hari who defeated the asuras, and as the one who beat Brahma in anger and himself created the world.
9.nuance: The life is told as one breathless sequence that runs from womb to women to disease with no pause, so that youth and lust lead straight to sickness. அயனையும் புடைத்துச் சினந்து உலகமும் படைத்து is the story in which Murugan punished Brahma and took over creation.

10.reading: The poet describes how courtesans wound with kohl-dark eyes, catch a man with a smile and a net of talk, take him home with 'come in', and make love to him, and asks to be freed from the sorrow these deceiving young women cause. The praise is a battle in which the sea churns, the serpent's crowns crack and the demons' heads are heaped like mountains in fat and blood, and names Murugan as the younger brother of Ganapati and the son of the one who kicked Yama, at Parangiri.
10.nuance: சமன் உதைபட நிறுவிய பரன் is Siva who kicked Yama, the story of Markandeya; the song places it beside the poet's own fear without drawing the line. நஞ்சன சிறுமிகள் calls the women poisonous girls.

11.reading: A song mostly of praise: Murugan threw the blazing ball at the great golden mountain, was born as companion of the elephant, is nephew of the one who sleeps on the serpent and churned the sea, and son of the one who burned the three cities; with drums sounding he tore the bodies of the Suras and came on the peacock. In its middle the poet, small, base and a killer, troubled by many sorrows, asks Murugan to come and end his birth today, at Parangiri.
11.nuance: சிறியன் புலையன் கொலையன் is the self-description of the book: small, outcast, killer. The ball thrown at the mountain (செண்டை எறிந்திடு) is an allusion I cannot place with certainty.

12.reading: The poet tells how Kama, with eyes like carp, the five senses and the moon, attacks with his bow and how, deluded, he follows women and suffers in their embrace; he asks instead for the feet that devotees adorn with kadamba garlands. The praise names Murugan as the one who struck the lotus-dweller's head and fettered him and told the wealth of knowledge to Siva, whose twelve shoulders the conch-necked daughter of Indra and the hunter girl embrace, and who destroyed the clan of Nirudan, at south Parangundram.
12.nuance: மயல் (delusion) is the poet's word for his state. Brahma (போதிலுறைந்தருள்கின்றவன்) is struck and bound, and the knowledge he lacked is given to Siva (போதவளம் சிவசங்கரன் கொண்டிட மொழிவோனே), the same story as 6. One word is corrupt; கிரீவ, neck, is the likely reading.

13.reading: A short song: the poet asks whether, no longer wandering anxious in the chain of bonds, he will one day call on Kanda again and again, see him and love him. He names Murugan as the one joined to the elephant's daughter, the son of Sivai on Sankara's side, the vel at Senthil and Kandi, the lord at south Parangundram.
13.nuance: பந்தத் தொடர், the chain of bonds, and சஞ்சலம், agitation, are the condition; the cure is only the repeated name கந்தன். கண்டிக் கதிர்வேலா may point to Kathirkamam in Lanka; the reading is uncertain.

14.reading: The poet, sick with love, says that Kama's arrows, the burning moon, women's eyes, the south wind from the grove and the cuckoo singing night and day have kept his eyes from sleep, and asks whether a deceiver like him, wasted by infatuation, can now reach Murugan's blossoming feet. The praise names Vishnu who ate curd in the cowherds' homes and walked behind those who study Tamil, and Murugan as his nephew, at Parangiri where moon, sun and cloud move.
14.nuance: The love-sickness is told with the stock machinery of Tamil love poetry (moon, south wind, cuckoo, sleepless eyes), but its object is women in general and the speaker calls himself a deceiver (வஞ்சகன்). வண்டமிழ் பயில்வோர் பின் திரிகின்றவன் is Vishnu following a Tamil poet.

15.reading: The poet confesses that he has gone begging to people, praising them as lotus-handed, clouds in giving and the refuge of Tamil, his heart wounded and spinning like a top, and calls his body a swinging pot, a mass of suffering clay, a ship that sinks, a life of five senses; he asks Murugan to correct him in a moment and take him into service at his anklets. The praise names him the lone vel who set Brahma to create, Siva to destroy and Vishnu to protect, and ended the gods' fear, the son of Ganga at Parangundram, who folded his hands to the hunter girl in the millet field.
15.nuance: The confession is of a poet's trade: praising patrons in Tamil for gifts (தண்டமிழ்க்குத் தஞ்சம்). The plea is to exchange that service for தொண்டு, service at the Lord's feet. The body images (ஊசல் கடம், துன்ப மண் சடம், துஞ்சிடும் கலம்) stress its frailty. The praise also reverses rank: Murugan folds his hands before Valli.

16.reading: The poet describes the breasts, eyes and dark hair of women whom young men worship and confide in, women who undress and give the stronghold of pleasure, and calls himself a fool and madman caught by them; he asks for the lotus of Murugan's anklets to end the delusion of his mind. The praise names the vel that tore out the guts of the demon who hid in fear in the sea, the hunters' din in the millet field, and Murugan's embrace of the girl there, at Thiruparankundram.
16.nuance: இளைஞோர்கள் துதித்து முன் கும்பிட்டு: the young men worship the women, a reversal of worship that the plea sets right. The hunters' drum and horn syllables (குகுக்குகு, திதித்தி) fill two lines.

17.reading: The poet speaks of deceitful courtesans with mountainous breasts who take a man's wealth, quarrel and leave, and asks what he gains by wearing out his body after them, and whether Murugan's lotus feet will not love him. The praise names him Kandavel whom Brahma, Vishnu and Siva worship, the one of the Tamil mouth who set the hard Jains on great stakes, and the one who went to the hunter girl in the millet field, at Thiruparankundram.
17.nuance: பொருட்கவர்ந்து, taking wealth, marks them as courtesans. வன்சமணரைப் பெருந்திண்கழு மிசைக்கிடும் செந்தமிழ் அங்கவாயா identifies Murugan with the Tamil saint who defeated the Jains at Madurai (Sambandar, by tradition), a claim the book repeats.

18.reading: The poet speaks of women whose hair the bees follow and whose lips and breasts draw him until he falls into the pool of the navel, and asks to be joined to Murugan's feet with their anklets and bells. The praise names him the son of Siva who wears the boar's tusk, the tortoise shell, serpents and the gods' bones, the younger brother of the five-handed scholar, the lord of Vayalur who took the girl the hill people gave, at south Parangundram.
18.nuance: உந்தி என்கின்ற மடு, the pool called the navel, is the image of drowning. One word is corrupt; வயலூரா is clear from context.

19.reading: The poet describes courtesans who bewitch young men with breasts and smiles, invite them home, and while robbing them of wealth make them fall into their laps, and calls himself the small fool who trusted their false minds; he asks whether there is any thought of granting such a one grace. The praise names the vel, the hunter girl whom Murugan embraced, Rama who bridged the sea and slew Lanka's demons with one arrow as his uncle, and Murugan as Saravanabhava and guru, at Parangiri.
19.nuance: கணிகையர் தமதுபொய் மனத்தை நம்பிய: the fault is trusting, and the women's deceit and greed (வண்பொருள் கவர்பொழுதினில்) are the stock charge of the Kural and Naladiyar chapters on courtesans.

20.reading: The poet says that through women's breasts, bangled hands, eyes, lips and hair he has fallen into their power and is perishing like cotton in fire, and asks for Murugan's lotus feet with tinkling anklets so that he may cross the sea of bonds. The praise names the vel thrown at Sura, who harmed the gods and destroyed Indra's world, and at Krauncha, Vishnu with the conch as his uncle, and the hunter girl, at Thiruparankundram.
20.nuance: தொந்த வாரி, the sea of bonds, and கரையேற, to reach the shore: the feet are a crossing. One word is corrupt; புண்டரீகம் (lotus) is clear from context.

links.note: Both set the Lord against Death's messengers at the hour of death. Tirumular says those who think of the Lord will not be harmed by them; 8 is the prayer of one who has not done the thinking and asks Murugan to come anyway, on the peacock, at that moment.

The Kural says the heart melts at the thought of begging; 15 confesses the act, a poet praising patrons as Tamil's refuge 'with a wounded heart', and asks to trade that service for service at Murugan's feet.
Both describe women who want a man for his wealth and whose sweet invitations harm him; the Kural warns, 19 confesses to having trusted them.
Both make Murugan Siva's teacher: in 6 he teaches what precedes the Veda, in 12 he punishes Brahma and gives the knowledge to Siva.

Thiruppugazh 7 describes lovemaking at length and asks only whether he will ever give up delighting in it (கனகலவியை மகிழ்வது தவிர்வேனோ), so that giving it up is the condition of grace. Thiruppugazh 153 describes the same scene, bird-cries of the throat included, and says that even if he falls into that river of pleasure (அநுபோக நதியினிடை வீழுகினும) he will not forget the feet for a moment. On the reading that 7 makes renunciation the way to Murugan, 153 holds that devotion can survive the pleasure without it.

Tirumanthiram 163 compresses a life into three numbers: the egg born in three hundred days, marriage at twelve, ruin at seventy (கெட்டது எழுபதில் கேடறியீரே). Thiruppugazh 9 runs the same course stage by stage, ten months in the womb (கருவடைந்து பத்துற்ற திங்கள்), nursing, crawling, ornaments, youth, women and wandering in disease. The song spells out what the Tirumanthiram's count leaves implicit, and both end in decay that the person does not see coming.

Kural 918 says the embrace of deceiving women (மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு) is an afflicting spirit to those without discerning understanding. Thiruppugazh 10 shows that embrace from the inside: the kohl eyes, the smile, the net of talk, 'come in' (மனைக்கு எழுந்திரும்), the bed, and then the plea to be freed from the sorrow of these poisonous girls (நஞ்சன சிறுமிகள் துயரற). The song is the experience the Kural's verdict describes.

Kural 329 says those whose work is killing (கொலைவினையர்) are base in their work (புலைவினையர்) to those who discern. Thiruppugazh 11, asking Murugan to end his birth today, names himself small, base, a killer (சிறியன் புலையன் கொலையன்), setting புலையன் beside கொலையன் as the Kural joins them. The poet passes on himself the judgment the Kural passes on killers.

Thiruppugazh 13 asks whether, no longer agitated in the chain of bonds, he will call 'Kanda' again and again (கந்தனென் றென்றுற்று), see him and love him. Tirumanthiram 278 says men call the Lord 'our father, our Lord' (எந்தை பிரானென்று) inside their wants and do not seek him with longing (நச்சியே ... நாடுகிலாரே). The Tirumanthiram adds the condition the song's plea implies: the repeated name counts only when it carries love rather than want.

Naladiyar 44 refuses to be moved by blind, petty men (கண்ணில் புன்மாக்கள்) who call eyes lilies, carp and spears. Thiruppugazh 16 gives those men's praise in full, eyes like carp (கயல் ஒக்கும் பருத்தகண்), hair like darkness, breasts like golden pots, and says the young men worship the women (இளைஞோர்கள் துதித்து முன் கும்பிட்டு), then calls himself a madman caught by them. The Naladiyar's speaker stands outside the comparisons; the poet confesses being inside them.

Thiruppugazh 17 speaks of women who take a man's wealth and pick a quarrel (பொருட்கவர்ந்து ஒன்றிய பிணக்கிடும் சண்டிகள்) and asks what he gains by wearing out his body after them. Naladiyar 372 shows the quarrel's pretext: the woman who swore to leap from the peak with him found, when he had no gold, a pain in her feet (காற்கால்நோய் காட்டி) and stayed behind. Both tie the courtesan's company to the money and her excuse to its running out.

Tirumanthiram 371 says the Lord rose bearing bones and a skull, and that without his bearing them they would have fallen to dust; whose bones they are it leaves to tradition. Thiruppugazh 18 names Siva as the one who wears the boar's tusk, the tortoise shell, serpents and the old bones of the gods (சுரர்கள் பண்டை என்பு அங்கம் அணிபவர்). The song states plainly the reading the Tirumanthiram's nuance can only attribute to tradition: the bones are the gods' own.

Thiruppugazh 19 calls himself the small fool who trusted the false minds of the courtesans (கணிகையர் தமதுபொய் மனத்தை நம்பிய சிறியனை) while they seized his wealth. Naladiyar 377 says those fooled into thinking such a woman's love their own (ஏமாந்து எமதென்று இருந்தார்), while she takes the wealth from their hands, will be laughed at by many. The fault in both is the trust, not only the women's greed.

Thiruppugazh 20 says that, overcome by women, he perishes like cotton caught in fire (எரிப்படும் பஞ்சு போல மிகக்கெடும் தொண்டனேனும்). Tirumanthiram 117 uses the same cotton for the opposite: the sunstone burns the surrounding cotton only in the sun's presence, as the malas end before the Lord. In the song the self is the cotton that burns; in the Tirumanthiram the impurity is, and its burning is release.

Thiruppugazh 20 asks for Murugan's lotus feet so that he may reach the shore of the sea of bonds (தொந்த வாரி கரையேற). Tirumanthiram 1498 says the rare shore is the shade of the Lord's feet (அருங்கரை யாவது அவ்வடி நீழல்), the one shore for all souls coming toward it. Both make the feet the shore of a sea; the song names the sea as bonds, which the Tirumanthiram leaves unnamed.

source_issues: Song 10: one corrupt character in மிடறு஡டே (line 9); probably மிடறூடே.
Song 12: one corrupt character in கி஡ணவ (line 16); probably கிரீவ (neck).
Song 18: one corrupt character in வயலு஡ரா (line 12); clearly வயலூரா.
Song 20: one corrupt character in புண்ட஡ணகம் (line 12); clearly புண்டரீகம். The source's ஡ appears to stand for ஊ or ரீ in different songs.
